1_statement.original:
\label{prop:freeproduct}
There is a group $\mathop{\ast}_\alpha G_\alpha$, the \emph{free product}, whose elements are the reduced words, in which each $G_\alpha$ sits as the words of length at most $1$, and in which the
product of $g_1\cdots g_m$ and $h_1\cdots h_n$ is obtained from the concatenation by repeatedly multiplying adjacent letters from the same group and deleting identities. It has the
universal property: homomorphisms $\varphi_\alpha\colon G_\alpha\to K$ extend uniquely to a homomorphism $\mathop{\ast}_\alpha G_\alpha\to K$.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{prop:freeproduct}
The reduced words form a group $\mathop{\ast}_\alpha G_\alpha$, the \emph{free product}. Each factor embeds as words of length at most one. To multiply, concatenate words, multiply adjacent letters from the same factor and delete identities until the word is reduced. Homomorphisms $\varphi_\alpha:G_\alpha\to K$ extend uniquely to a homomorphism $\mathop{\ast}_\alpha G_\alpha\to K$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
We must justify that reduction gives an associative operation. For $g\in G_\alpha$, let $L_g$ act on $W$ by inserting $g$ on the left and doing the required first reduction. If $g=1$, do nothing. If the first letter is in another factor, prepend $g$. If it is $a\in G_\alpha$, replace it by $ga$, deleting it when $ga=1$.

For $g,h\in G_\alpha$, we have $L_gL_h=L_{gh}$. To check this, first take a word empty or beginning in a different factor: prepending $h$ and then combining $g$ with it gives $gh$, with deletion if needed. For a word $aw'$ beginning in $G_\alpha$, if $ha\ne1$, both procedures replace $a$ by $g(ha)=(gh)a$, deleting an identity. If $ha=1$, the first procedure removes $a$, then prepends $g$ to $w'$, whose first factor is different. The second combines $(gh)a=g$ and gives the same result. Cases with identity letters are included by $L_1=\mathrm{id}$. Thus $L_g$ is a permutation with inverse $L_{g^{-1}}$.

Let $P$ be the group generated by these permutations. Combining adjacent operators from the same factor expresses every member as $L_{g_1}\cdots L_{g_m}$ for a reduced word. Applied to the empty word, this permutation returns $g_1\cdots g_m$. Different reduced words therefore give different permutations. Transporting the group law of $P$ to $W$ proves the asserted multiplication and associativity.

Finally send a reduced word to $\varphi(g_1)\cdots\varphi(g_m)$ in $K$. Each allowed reduction leaves this value unchanged because each $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homomorphism. Thus the map respects products. Its values on the factors force uniqueness. If there are no nontrivial factors, only the empty word remains, giving the trivial group.

Finally send a reduced word to $\varphi(g_1)\cdots\varphi(g_m)$ in $K$. Each allowed reduction leaves this value unchanged because each $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homomorphism. 4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
A loop can pass between $U$ and $V$ away from $x_0$. We first connect each passage back to $x_0$ to obtain based loops. Subdivide a loop $f$ into finitely many paths $f_i$ lying in $A_i\in\{U,V\}$, using a Lebesgue number on $I$. At the joining points choose paths $g_i$ from $x_0$ inside $A_i\cap A_{i+1}$; take the two endpoint paths constant. Then
\[
f\simeq(f_1\bar g_1)(g_1f_2\bar g_2)\cdots(g_{m-1}f_m).
\]
Each factor lies in one of the two sets. This proves surjectivity. The generators of $N$ project to the identity because the two inclusions of $U\cap V$ into $X$ are the same, so $N\subset\ker\Phi$.

Put $Q=(\pi_1(U)\ast\pi_1(V))/N$. Combining adjacent loops in one set does not change their product in $Q$. A loop in $U\cap V$ can also be regarded as a loop in either set without changing its value in $Q$. We show that these facts make any two factorizations of the same loop class equal in $Q$.

Represent the two factorizations by loops $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ and $f'_1,\ldots,f'_l$, assigning equal time to the pieces as justified earlier. Replace an empty factorization by a constant loop, so $k,l\ge1$. Let $F$ be a based homotopy between the concatenations. Only the left and right edges of its square are necessarily constant. Along the bottom and top, $F$ returns to $x_0$ at the factor joins $i/k$ and $j/l$.

Take a common vertical subdivision through all those joins, then refine both directions until every rectangle $R$ maps into a chosen $A(R)\in\{U,V\}$. At each grid vertex $v$, choose a path $g_v$ from $x_0$ to $F(v)$ inside all incident $A(R)$ and, on the bottom or top, inside the sets containing the corresponding factor loops. This is possible: every such intersection is $U$, $V$ or $U\cap V$, is path-connected, and contains both endpoints. Choose $g_v$ constant whenever $F(v)=x_0$, in particular on the left and right sides and at factor joins.

For an oriented grid edge from $v$ to $w$, let
\[
L(v,w)=g_v\cdot F|_{[v,w]}\cdot\bar g_w.
\]
It lies in every incident rectangle's chosen set and in the appropriate boundary factor set. If these choices differ, the loop lies in $U\cap V$ and has the same value in $Q$ with either interpretation.

In one rectangle, the products associated with its bottom-right and left-top routes agree in $\pi_1(A(R))$. Cancel the middle $g$ paths; the remaining two routes are homotopic through $F$ on the rectangle. Consequently swapping these routes does not change a grid path's product in $Q$. Successively swapping across the finitely many rectangles changes the route along the bottom and right sides into the route along the left and top sides.

The initial product equals the first factorization: the right-side loops are constant, and the bottom-edge pieces within a factor combine in that factor's set; their connector paths cancel and the factor endpoints have constant connectors. The final product equals the second factorization for the same reason. The two words therefore agree in $Q$. Apply this to a word in $\ker\Phi$ and the constant factorization. Its class in $Q$ is the identity, so it belongs to $N$.

1_statement.original:
\label{ex:surfaces}
Glue the sides of a $4g$-gon in the pattern
\[a_1b_1a_1^{-1}b_1^{-1}\cdots a_gb_ga_g^{-1}b_g^{-1}:\]
the result is the closed orientable surface $\Sigma_g$ of genus $g$ (for $g=1$, the square with opposite
sides glued, the torus). All vertices of the polygon become one point, and the edges become $2g$ circles through it, a wedge of $2g$ circles; the inside of the polygon is a disc attached along
the word. By Proposition~\ref{prop:attachdisc} and Theorem~\ref{thm:wedge} below,
\[\pi_1(\Sigma_g)\cong\bigl\langle a_1,b_1,\dots,a_g,b_g\mid[a_1,b_1]\cdots[a_g,b_g]\bigr\rangle,\qquad[a,b]=aba^{-1}b^{-1},\]
the quotient of the free group by the normal subgroup generated by the relator. Making the group abelian kills the relator and gives $\Z^{2g}$, so surfaces of different genus have
non-isomorphic fundamental groups and are not homeomorphic, nor even homotopy equivalent. For $g=1$ we recover $\Z^2$. The projective plane is a disc with antipodal boundary points identified,
a circle $a$ with a disc attached along $a^2$: $\pi_1(\R P^2)=\Z/2$, as in Example~\ref{ex:computations}.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{ex:surfaces}
For $g\ge1$, identify the sides of a $4g$-gon in the order
\[
a_1b_1a_1^{-1}b_1^{-1}\cdots a_gb_ga_g^{-1}b_g^{-1}.
\]
The result is the closed orientable surface $\Sigma_g$. Its vertices become one point, its edges a bouquet of $2g$ circles, and its interior an attached disc. The bouquet computation and the proposition give
\[
\pi_1(\Sigma_g)\cong
\langle a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_g,b_g\mid [a_1,b_1]\cdots[a_g,b_g]\rangle,
\qquad [a,b]=aba^{-1}b^{-1}.
\]
This presentation means the free group modulo the normal closure of the displayed word. Its \emph{abelianization}, the quotient by all commutators, is $\Z^{2g}$: after commuting the generators, the relator imposes no further relation, and the free abelian universal property gives the identification. Different genera have different abelianization ranks, hence different fundamental groups. They cannot be homeomorphic or homotopy equivalent. For $g=1$ the relation says $ab=ba$, recovering $\Z^2$. For $g=0$ the surface is $S^2$ and its group is trivial, consistent with no generators.

The projective plane has one circular edge $a$ and a disc whose boundary reads $a^2$, because antipodal boundary points are identified. Its group is therefore $\langle a\mid a^2\rangle=\Z/2$, agreeing with the sphere covering.

1_statement.original:
\label{thm:wedge}
Let $X$ be a finite connected graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges, $T$ a spanning tree, and $x_0$ a vertex. For each edge $e$ not in $T$, oriented from $u$ to $w$, let $\gamma_e$ be the loop that goes in
$T$ from $x_0$ to $u$, along $e$, and back in $T$ to $x_0$. Then $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is the free group on the classes $[\gamma_e]$, of rank $E-V+1$. In particular $\pi_1$ of a wedge of $n$ circles (one
vertex, $n$ loop edges) is $F_n$.

Induct on the number of edges outside $T$. With none, the graph is a contractible finite tree. Otherwise choose $e\notin T$ and remove its midpoint to obtain $U$. Let $V'$ be the open edge $e^\circ$ together with the open $1/3$-neighbourhood of $T$ in $X$. The set $U$ retracts onto $X'=X\setminus e^\circ$. The set $V'$ retracts onto $T\cup e$, a tree with one extra edge; its group is generated by $[\gamma_e]$. Indeed its unique circle is traversed once by that loop, with tree paths before and after. The intersection $U\cap V'$ retracts onto $T$: all its other pieces are short edge stubs, including the two halves of $e$ without the midpoint. All three sets are path-connected. Van Kampen gives
\[
\pi_1(X,x_0)\cong\pi_1(X',x_0)\ast\langle[\gamma_e]\rangle.
\]
Induction gives the claimed free basis. There are $E-(V-1)$ edges outside the spanning tree.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
The coset graph $X_H$ covers $R_n$, and injectivity of the induced map identifies $\pi_1(X_H)$ with $H$. If the index is $k<\infty$, there are $k$ vertices and $nk$ edges. The graph theorem gives rank $nk-k+1$. When $n=0$, the only subgroup has $k=1$ and rank zero, as the formula says.

For infinite index, $X_H$ is countable and locally finite. Root it at $H$. At every other vertex choose one edge to a vertex one step nearer the root. Following chosen edges reaches the root, so they connect all vertices. They have no circle: a vertex farthest from the root on such a circle would have to choose both incident circle edges, since both would go to nearer vertices. Thus they form a spanning tree $T$.

Every compact subset of this locally finite unit-edge graph lies in a finite subgraph. The open unit balls centred at vertices cover it, a finite subcollection suffices, and each such ball meets only finitely many edges. Given such a finite subgraph and any finitely many specified edges, add the finitely many tree paths from their vertices to the root. The result is a finite connected graph $Y$ with spanning tree $T\cap Y$.

A loop has compact image, so it lies in such a $Y$ and is a word in the loops $\gamma_e$ for edges outside $T$. These loops therefore generate the whole group. If a nonempty reduced word in them contracted in $X_H$, put the compact image of its contraction, together with its edges and root paths, in another such $Y$. 4_proof_steps.reviewed_proof:
The coset graph $X_H$ covers $R_n$, and injectivity of the induced map identifies $\pi_1(X_H)$ with $H$. If the index is $k<\infty$, there are $k$ vertices and $nk$ edges. The graph theorem gives rank $nk-k+1$. When $n=0$, the only subgroup has $k=1$ and rank zero, as the formula says.

For infinite index, $X_H$ is countable and locally finite. Root it at $H$. At every other vertex choose one edge to a vertex one step nearer the root. Following chosen edges reaches the root, so they connect all vertices. They have no circle: a vertex farthest from the root on such a circle would have to choose both incident circle edges, since both would go to nearer vertices. Thus they form a spanning tree $T$.

Every compact subset of this locally finite unit-edge graph lies in a finite subgraph. The open unit balls centred at vertices cover it, a finite subcollection suffices, and each such ball meets only finitely many edges. Given such a finite subgraph and any finitely many specified edges, add the finitely many tree paths from their vertices to the root. The result is a finite connected graph $Y$ with spanning tree $T\cap Y$.

A loop has compact image, so it lies in such a $Y$ and is a word in the loops $\gamma_e$ for edges outside $T$. These loops therefore generate the whole group. If a nonempty reduced word in them contracted in $X_H$, put the compact image of its contraction, together with its edges and root paths, in another such $Y$. The finite graph theorem says those generators are free there, a contradiction. Hence the loops outside $T$ are a free basis.

1_statement.original:
A \emph{chain complex} $C$ is a sequence of abelian groups and homomorphisms $\cdots\to C_{k+1}\xrightarrow{\partial}C_k\xrightarrow{\partial}C_{k-1}\to\cdots$ with $\partial\circ\partial=0$, and $C_k=0$ for $k<0$.
Elements of $Z_k=\ker(\partial\colon C_k\to C_{k-1})$ are \emph{cycles}, elements of $B_k=\partial(C_{k+1})$ are \emph{boundaries}, and the \emph{homology} is $H_k(C)=Z_k/B_k$. A \emph{chain map}
$f\colon C\to C'$ is a family of homomorphisms with $\partial f=f\partial$; it maps cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries, hence induces $f_*\colon H_k(C)\to H_k(C')$. Two chain maps
$f,g$ are \emph{chain homotopic} if there are $P\colon C_k\to C'_{k+1}$ with $\partial P+P\partial=g-f$; then $f_*=g_*$, because for a cycle $z$, $g(z)-f(z)=\partial P(z)$ is a boundary.
1_statement.reviewed:
A \emph{chain complex} is a sequence of abelian groups $C_k$ and homomorphisms $\partial:C_k\to C_{k-1}$ with $\partial^2=0$; unless an augmentation is specified, $C_k=0$ for $k<0$. Its \emph{cycles} are $Z_k=\ker\partial$, its \emph{boundaries} are $B_k=\partial C_{k+1}$, and its \emph{homology} is
\[
H_k(C)=Z_k/B_k.
\]
A \emph{chain map} $f:C\to C'$ commutes with $\partial$, and therefore induces $f_*:H_k(C)\to H_k(C')$. Maps $f,g$ are \emph{chain homotopic} if maps $P:C_k\to C'_{k+1}$ satisfy $\partial P+P\partial=g-f$.

1_statement.original:
\label{lem:zigzag}
A short exact sequence of chain complexes $0\to A\xrightarrow iB\xrightarrow jC\to0$ gives a long exact sequence
\[\cdots\to H_k(A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H_k(B)\xrightarrow{j_*}H_k(C)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{k-1}(A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H_{k-1}(B)\to\cdots\to H_0(C)\to0,\]
where $\delta[c]=[a]$ for $c=j(b)$ and $i(a)=\partial b$. It is natural: a commutative diagram of short exact sequences gives a commutative diagram of long exact sequences.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{lem:zigzag}
A short exact sequence of chain complexes $0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{j}C\to0$ induces the long exact sequence
\[
\cdots\to H_k(A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H_k(B)\xrightarrow{j_*}H_k(C)
\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{k-1}(A)\to\cdots\to H_0(C)\to0.
\]
For a cycle $c=j(b)$, the connecting map is $\delta[c]=[a]$, where $i(a)=\partial b$. A commutative diagram of short exact sequences induces a commutative diagram of these long sequences.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Lift the cycle $c$ to $b$. Since $j\partial b=\partial c=0$, exactness gives a unique $a$ with $i(a)=\partial b$. Also $i\partial a=\partial^2b=0$, so $a$ is a cycle. Changing $b$ by $i(a')$ changes $a$ by $\partial a'$. Changing $c$ by a boundary $\partial c'$ permits a change of $b$ by $\partial b'$ with $j(b')=c'$, which leaves $\partial b$ unchanged. These facts prove that $\delta$ is well defined and additive.

At $H_k(B)$, $j_*i_*=0$. If $b$ is a cycle and $j(b)=\partial c'$, lift $c'$ to $b'$; then $b-\partial b'=i(a)$ and injectivity of $i$ makes $a$ a cycle. Thus $[b]=i_*[a]$.

At $H_k(C)$, a projected cycle has zero connecting class. Conversely, if $\delta[c]=0$, write $a=\partial a'$; the lift $b-i(a')$ is a cycle projecting to $c$.

At $H_{k-1}(A)$, $i_*\delta[c]=[\partial b]=0$. Conversely, if $i(a)=\partial b$, then $c=j(b)$ is a cycle and $\delta[c]=[a]$. These three verifications establish exactness at every position, including the end because the complexes vanish in negative degrees. Every choice in the construction can be pushed through a commutative chain diagram, giving naturality.

\label{lem:five}
In a commutative diagram of abelian groups with exact rows
\[\begin{array}{ccccccccc}A_1&\to&A_2&\to&A_3&\to&A_4&\to&A_5\\ \downarrow\alpha_1&&\downarrow\alpha_2&&\downarrow\alpha_3&&\downarrow\alpha_4&&\downarrow\alpha_5\\ B_1&\to&B_2&\to&B_3&\to&B_4&\to&B_5\end{array}\]
if $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_4,\alpha_5$ are isomorphisms, so is $\alpha_3$.

For surjectivity, take $w\in B_3$ and write $g_3(w)=\alpha_4(u)$. Since $\alpha_5f_4(u)=g_4g_3(w)=0$, injectivity of $\alpha_5$ and exactness give $u=f_3(x)$. Then $w-\alpha_3(x)\in\ker g_3=\operatorname{im}g_2$. Surjectivity of $\alpha_2$ writes this difference as $g_2\alpha_2(y)=\alpha_3f_2(y)$. Thus $w=\alpha_3(x+f_2(y))$.

1_statement.original:
A (finite, ordered) \emph{simplicial complex} $K$ is a finite totally ordered set of vertices and a family of nonempty subsets, the \emph{simplices}, containing all singletons and all
nonempty subsets of its members. A simplex with $k+1$ vertices has dimension $k$ and is written $[v_0,\dots,v_k]$ with $v_0<\dots<v_k$. Its \emph{realization} is the convex hull of the
corresponding basis vectors of $\R^{\text{vertices}}$, and $|K|$ is the union of these, a compact space. A \emph{subcomplex} is a subfamily that is itself a simplicial complex. A
\emph{triangulation} of a space $X$ is a homeomorphism $|K|\to X$.
1_statement.reviewed: A finite ordered \emph{simplicial complex} $K$ consists of a finite totally ordered vertex set and a family of nonempty vertex subsets, called \emph{simplices}, containing every singleton and every nonempty subset of each member. A \emph{subcomplex} is a subfamily satisfying the same closure rule on its own vertices. A \emph{triangulation} of $X$ is a homeomorphism $|K|\to X$.

1_statement.original:
\label{prop:smithhomology}
Let $c_k$ be the number of $k$-simplices, $r_k$ the rank of $\partial\colon C_k\to C_{k-1}$, and $d_1\mid\dots\mid d_{r_{k+1}}$ the nonzero invariant factors of $\partial\colon C_{k+1}\to C_k$. Then
\[H^\Delta_k(K;\Z)\cong\Z^{b_k}\oplus\bigoplus_{d_i>1}\Z/d_i,\qquad b_k=c_k-r_k-r_{k+1}.\]
Consequently (the Euler--Poincar\'e formula)
\[\chi(K):=\sum_k(-1)^kc_k=\sum_k(-1)^kb_k.\]

\label{prop:smithhomology}

\[
H_k^\Delta(K;\Z)\cong\Z^{b_k}\oplus\bigoplus_{d_i>1}\Z/d_i,
\qquad b_k=c_k-r_k-r_{k+1}.
\]
In particular the Euler--Poincar\'e formula is
\[
\chi(K):=\sum_k(-1)^kc_k=\sum_k(-1)^kb_k.
\]

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Choose Smith bases $f_j$ of $C_{k+1}$ and $e_i$ of $C_k$, so $\partial f_i=d_ie_i$ for $i\le r=r_{k+1}$ and the other $f_j$ map to zero. Because $C_{k-1}$ is torsion-free, $d_i\partial e_i=0$ implies $\partial e_i=0$. Thus
\[
Z_k=\bigoplus_{i\le r}\Z e_i\ \oplus\
\left(Z_k\cap\operatorname{span}_{\Z}\{e_{r+1},\ldots,e_{c_k}\}\right).
\]
The second summand is free, by the subgroup theorem for free abelian groups in Volume~3, and has rank $c_k-r_k-r$. Dividing the first summand by $B_k=\bigoplus_{i\le r}d_i\Z e_i$ gives the cyclic factors. Factors with $d_i=1$ vanish. In the finite alternating sum, each $r_k$ occurs twice with opposite signs, giving the formula for $\chi$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
A singular $0$-simplex is a point. The boundary of a path from $x$ to $y$ is $[y]-[x]$. Sending each point to its path component therefore kills boundaries and maps onto the free module on those components. Its kernel consists of finite point sums with total coefficient zero in each component. Join each of the finitely many points to a chosen point of its component; their differences are path boundaries, so the kernel is precisely $B_0$. This is a direct sum, even with infinitely many components.

For a one-point space there is one singular simplex $\sigma_k$ in each degree. Its boundary is $\sigma_{k-1}$ for positive even $k$ and zero for odd $k$, since the alternating sum of $k+1$ signs is respectively one or zero. The augmentation $C_0\to R$ is the identity. This alternating complex is exact, proving the reduced assertion.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Let $F:X\times I\to Y$ join $f$ to $g$. For $\sigma:\Delta^k\to X$ write $v_i=(e_i,0)$, $w_i=(e_i,1)$ and $\Phi=F\circ(\sigma\times\mathrm{id})$. Define the \emph{prism operator}
\[
P\sigma=\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\Phi|[v_0,\ldots,v_i,w_i,\ldots,w_k].
\]
For $k=0$ this is the path tracing the homotopy of a point. For general $k$, the terms triangulate the prism over $\Delta^k$ with consistent signs. We check the boundary identity rather than assuming it from the picture.

Deleting a bottom vertex $v_j$, $j\le i$, contributes sign $(-1)^{i+j}$. Deleting a top vertex $w_j$, $j\ge i$, contributes $(-1)^{i+j+1}$. The diagonal face obtained by deleting $v_i$ in prism $i$ has sign $+1$ and cancels the same face obtained by deleting $w_{i-1}$ in prism $i-1$, with sign $-1$. At the two ends this leaves $g\sigma-f\sigma$. All other faces lie over a proper face of $\Delta^k$. If its missing index is $j<i$, its prism index becomes $i-1$, and its sign in $P\partial\sigma$ is $(-1)^{j+i-1}$, opposite to the boundary sign. If $j>i$, its prism index stays $i$, giving sign $(-1)^{j+i}$, again opposite. Thus
\[
\partial P+P\partial=g_\#-f_\#.
\]
This chain homotopy proves $f_*=g_*$. Homotopy inverses then induce inverse homology maps. A contraction is a homotopy equivalence to a point, whose reduced groups we have computed.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
First work with affine singular simplices $\lambda=[w_0,\ldots,w_k]$ in a convex subset of Euclidean space; repeated vertices are allowed. For $b$ in that set, the cone $b\lambda=[b,w_0,\ldots,w_k]$ obeys
\[
\partial(b\lambda)=\lambda-b\partial\lambda\quad(k\ge1),\qquad
\partial(b\lambda)=\lambda-\varepsilon(\lambda)[b]\quad(k=0).
\]
These follow by deleting the first vertex and then the remaining vertices with their signs. Let $b_\lambda$ be the barycentre. Define subdivision $S$ and a homotopy $T$ inductively:
\[
S\lambda=\lambda\ (k=0),\quad S\lambda=b_\lambda(S\partial\lambda)\ (k>0),
\qquad
T\lambda=0\ (k=0),\quad T\lambda=b_\lambda(\lambda-T\partial\lambda)\ (k>0).
\]
The cone identity and induction give $\partial S=S\partial$. For $k=1$ the augmentation terms in $S\partial\lambda$ cancel, as the coefficients of a boundary sum to zero. In higher degrees $\partial S\partial\lambda=0$ gives the same conclusion. For $T$, the induction identity on the boundary gives
\[
\partial T\lambda
=\lambda-T\partial\lambda-b_\lambda(\partial\lambda-\partial T\partial\lambda)
=\lambda-T\partial\lambda-b_\lambda S\partial\lambda
=\lambda-T\partial\lambda-S\lambda.
\]
Thus $\partial T+T\partial=\mathrm{id}-S$. It also holds in degree zero because $S=\mathrm{id}$ there.

The vertices of each subdivided simplex are barycentres of a nested sequence of faces. If $F\subset G$ and $G$ has dimension $j\le k$, then
\[
|b_G-b_F|\le\max_{w\text{ vertex of }G}|b_G-w|
\le\frac{j}{j+1}\operatorname{diam}G
\le\frac{k}{k+1}\operatorname{diam}\lambda.
\]
The middle bound follows from $b_G-w=(j+1)^{-1}\sum_{w'\ne w}(w'-w)$. Hence subdivision in positive dimension shrinks diameters by at most $k/(k+1)$; repeated subdivision makes them tend to zero.

For arbitrary $\sigma:\Delta^k\to X$, perform these constructions on the identity simplex of $\Delta^k$ and compose all terms with $\sigma$. Affine maps preserve barycentres, so face restrictions commute with the construction. We obtain the same identities $\partial S=S\partial$ and $\partial T+T\partial=\mathrm{id}-S$ on singular chains. Both operators keep every term inside its original simplex image. With
\[
D_m=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}TS^i
\]
we have $\partial D_m+D_m\partial=\mathrm{id}-S^m$, also for $m=0$ with an empty sum.

Given a finite chain, choose $m$ large enough geometrically for all its simplices: the sets $\sigma^{-1}(\operatorname{int}U_j)$ cover each compact domain simplex, so a Lebesgue number and the diameter estimate put every subdivided piece inside some $U_j$. Choose this depth before any cancellation of terms. Zero-dimensional simplices are already small.

If $z$ is a cycle, such an $m$ makes $S^mz$ small and $z-S^mz=\partial D_mz$, proving surjectivity on homology. If a small cycle $z$ bounds $b$ in $C(X)$, choose $m$ making $S^mb$ small. Since $D_m$ preserves supports, $D_mz$ is small too, and
\[
z=S^mz+\partial D_mz=\partial(S^mb+D_mz)
\]
is a boundary in the small complex. This proves injectivity.

1_statement.original:
\label{thm:mv}
If $X=\operatorname{int}A\cup\operatorname{int}B$, there is a long exact sequence
\[\cdots\to H_n(A\cap B)\xrightarrow{(i_{A*},\,i_{B*})}H_n(A)\oplus H_n(B)\xrightarrow{j_{A*}-j_{B*}}H_n(X)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A\cap B)\to\cdots\]
with all maps induced by inclusions except $\delta$, and the same in reduced homology when $A\cap B\ne\emptyset$. If $z=x+y$ is a cycle with $x$ in $A$ and $y$ in $B$, then $\delta[z]=[\partial x]$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Induct on the number of simplices, starting with the empty complex, whose unaugmented chains vanish on both sides. Choose a maximal simplex $\sigma$ of dimension $d$, and let $L$ consist of all other simplices. It is a subcomplex because $\sigma$ is not a proper face of another simplex. Write $\bar\sigma$ for the complex of all its faces and $\partial\bar\sigma$ for its proper faces.

The comparison holds for the single simplex $\bar\sigma$ without induction. Its singular realization is convex. On simplicial augmented chains, coning to the first vertex, with a repeated first vertex interpreted as zero, gives $\partial h+h\partial=\mathrm{id}$ by the face formula. Equivalently its unaugmented homology is $R$ in degree zero and zero above, and $\varphi_*$ sends a vertex generator to the corresponding point generator. The boundary complex has fewer simplices than $K$, so induction and the pair sequences, with the five lemma, give the comparison for $(\bar\sigma,\partial\bar\sigma)$.

On simplicial relative chains, inclusion from this pair to $(K,L)$ is an isomorphism: only the generator $\sigma$ in degree $d$ remains. We verify the singular relative inclusion too. For $d=0$, $\sigma$ is an isolated point, and the singular chains split as the direct sum for that point and $|L|$, proving the claim directly. For $d>0$, let $b$ be the barycentre and $W=|K|\setminus\{b\}$. Radial projection from $b$ retracts $W$ onto $|L|$, fixing $|L|$; within $|\sigma|$ it retracts $|\sigma|\setminus\{b\}$ onto $|\partial\bar\sigma|$. The maps from the original pairs to these punctured pairs therefore induce isomorphisms.

Excision removes the closed set $|L|$ from $(|K|,W)$ and the closed boundary $|\partial\bar\sigma|$ from $(|\sigma|,|\sigma|\setminus\{b\})$. Both removed sets lie inside the relevant open punctured subspaces. The results are the same pair
\[
(\sigma^\circ,\sigma^\circ\setminus\{b\}).
\]
Here $\sigma^\circ$ is open in $|K|$ because $\sigma$ is maximal in a finite complex. Every map is induced by inclusion, so these identifications show that the singular inclusion of pairs is an isomorphism. In the comparison square, the other three maps are now isomorphisms, hence so is the map for $(K,L)$. The pair sequences and the induction hypothesis for $L$ give the result for $K$ by the five lemma. Finally, for any subcomplex pair, the two absolute comparisons and its pair sequences give the relative comparison.

\label{cor:euler}
The Betti numbers and Euler characteristic of a finite simplicial complex depend only on the homotopy type of its realization. \label{ex:surfacesH}
\emph{Loops and $H_1$.} A loop $\gamma$ is a singular $1$-simplex with $\partial\gamma=0$. If $\gamma,\delta$ are loops at the same point, the singular $2$-simplex that runs $\gamma$ on $[e_0,e_1]$, $\delta$ on $[e_1,e_2]$
and $\gamma\cdot\delta$ on $[e_0,e_2]$ (compose $\gamma\cdot\delta$ with the affine map $\Delta^2\to[0,1]$ sending $e_0,e_1,e_2$ to $0,\frac12,1$) has boundary $\delta-\gamma\cdot\delta+\gamma$; and a homotopy of loops gives, by the
prism operator, a homology. So $[\gamma]\mapsto[\gamma]$ is a homomorphism $h\colon\pi_1(X,x_0)\to H_1(X)$. For the circle, Mayer--Vietoris with two arcs gives $H_1(S^1)\cong\tilde H_0(\text{two points})=\Z$,
and the loop $\omega_1$ maps to a generator (its two halves give $\delta[\omega_1]=\pm([p]-[q])$). So $h$ is the isomorphism $\pi_1(S^1)\cong H_1(S^1)$, and the degree of a map of the circle is its winding number.

\emph{Surfaces.} By induction with Mayer--Vietoris, $H_1$ of a wedge of $n$ circles is $\Z^n$, generated by the images of the $n$ loops, and $H_2=0$. Let $\Sigma_g$ be the polygon model of
Example~\ref{ex:surfaces}, $V$ a small open disc in the polygon and $U$ the complement of its centre. Then $U$ deformation retracts onto the wedge of $2g$ circles, $V$ is contractible, and $U\cap V$
deformation retracts onto a circle, whose generator maps in $H_1(U)$ to $h$ of the boundary word, $a_1+b_1-a_1-b_1+\dots=0$. Reduced Mayer--Vietoris reads
\[0\to H_2(\Sigma_g)\to H_1(S^1)=\Z\xrightarrow{0}\Z^{2g}\to H_1(\Sigma_g)\to\tilde H_0(S^1)=0,\]
so $H_2(\Sigma_g)=\Z$, $H_1(\Sigma_g)=\Z^{2g}$, $H_0=\Z$, and $\chi(\Sigma_g)=2-2g$. This is the value of the index sum of Chapter~4 for the pretzel with $g$ holes, which is homeomorphic to
$\Sigma_g$ (this follows from the classification of surfaces, a remark here).
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{ex:surfacesH}
\emph{Turning loops into homology classes.} A loop is a singular $1$-cycle. For based loops $\gamma,\eta$, compose $\gamma\eta$ with the affine map $\Delta^2\to I$ taking its vertices to $0,1/2,1$. Its boundary is $\eta-\gamma\eta+\gamma$. Thus concatenation becomes addition in $H_1$. A based homotopy gives a homology by the prism operator; its constant side paths cancel. We obtain a homomorphism $h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\to H_1(X)$.

On $S^1$, cover by two open arcs with intersection two arcs. Mayer--Vietoris gives $H_1(S^1)\cong\tilde H_0(\text{two points})=\Z$. Subdividing a positive loop into its arc pieces sends it under $\delta$ to the difference of the two overlap components, a generator up to sign. Hence $h$ identifies the winding generator of $\pi_1(S^1)$ with a generator of $H_1(S^1)$. By naturality, a circle map's action on $H_1$ is multiplication by its winding number, so this is its degree.

\emph{Surface groups become abelian.} Use the bouquet open covers from Chapter~5 with Mayer--Vietoris. Their contractible star intersections show that a bouquet of $m$ circles has $H_1=\Z^m$, with its loops as generators, and all higher homology zero. For $\Sigma_g$, remove the polygon disc's centre to obtain $U$, retracting onto the bouquet of $2g$ circles, and take its open interior as $V$. The intersection retracts onto its boundary circle. The attaching word has homology class
\[
a_1+b_1-a_1-b_1+\cdots+a_g+b_g-a_g-b_g=0.
\]
Reduced Mayer--Vietoris therefore contains
\[
0\to H_2(\Sigma_g)\to\Z\xrightarrow{0}\Z^{2g}
\to H_1(\Sigma_g)\to0.
\]
It follows that $H_2=\Z$, $H_1=\Z^{2g}$, $H_0=\Z$, and all higher groups vanish. Thus $\chi(\Sigma_g)=2-2g$. For $g=0$ the sphere computation gives the same formula directly. This is also the index sum found in Chapter~4 for a smooth surface with $g$ handles.

\label{prop:jordanbrouwer}
Let $n\ge1$. (a) If $h\colon\bar B^k\to S^n$ is an embedding (a continuous injection; a homeomorphism onto its image, $\bar B^k$ being compact), then $\tilde H_i(S^n\setminus h(\bar B^k))=0$ for all $i$.
(b) If $h\colon S^k\to S^n$ is an embedding with $k<n$, then $\tilde H_i(S^n\setminus h(S^k))$ is $\Z$ for $i=n-k-1$ and $0$ otherwise. In particular (Jordan--Brouwer) the complement of an embedded $S^{n-1}$
in $S^n$ has exactly two path components, and the complement of an embedded ball is path-connected.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
(a) Replace the ball by the homeomorphic cube $I^k$. Its complement is nonempty: otherwise the embedding would identify a contractible cube with the noncontractible sphere, contrary to their homology. For $k=0$ the complement of a point is $\R^n$, so the assertion holds.

Induct on $k$. Suppose a nonzero reduced class $\alpha$ exists in the complement of $h(I^k)$. Cut the last coordinate interval in half. The complements of the two image half-cubes are open sets $A,B$ with
\[
A\cap B=S^n\setminus h(I^k),\qquad
A\cup B=S^n\setminus h(I^{k-1}\times\{1/2\}).
\]
Induction makes the reduced homology of the union zero. Mayer--Vietoris therefore makes $\tilde H_i(A\cap B)\to\tilde H_i(A)\oplus\tilde H_i(B)$ an isomorphism, so $\alpha$ remains nonzero in at least one half-cube complement. Repeating produces nested closed intervals $J_m$ of lengths $2^{-m}$, with intersection $\{p\}$, such that the class stays nonzero in each $S^n\setminus h(I^{k-1}\times J_m)$.

These increasing open complements have union $S^n\setminus h(I^{k-1}\times\{p\})$. The latter has zero reduced homology by induction, so a cycle representing $\alpha$ bounds a finite chain there. Its compact simplex images lie in one of the increasing complements: a finite subcover by these nested open sets suffices. It would then bound there already, a contradiction. In degree zero the cycle has augmentation zero and the same bounding argument applies; negative reduced degrees vanish because the complements are nonempty.

(b) For $k=0$, remove two points from $S^n$. The complement is $\R^n$ minus a point and retracts onto $S^{n-1}$. For $k\ge1$, divide $S^k$ into closed hemispheres $D_+,D_-$ meeting in $S^{k-1}$. The open sets $A=S^n\setminus h(D_+)$ and $B=S^n\setminus h(D_-)$ have zero reduced homology by (a). Their union is the complement of the equator image, and their intersection is the complement of $h(S^k)$. Mayer--Vietoris gives
\[
\tilde H_i(S^n\setminus h(S^k))
\cong\tilde H_{i+1}(S^n\setminus h(S^{k-1})).
\]
Induction proves the formula. Finally $\tilde H_0$ is free with one fewer generator than the number of path components when that number is finite; zero reduced $H_0$ for a nonempty space means one component, and $\tilde H_0=\Z$ means two. All complements here are open in $S^n$, hence locally path-connected, so these path components are open as well.

\label{thm:borsukulam}
For $n\ge1$ there is no continuous map $g\colon S^n\to S^{n-1}$ with $g(-x)=-g(x)$. Equivalently, every continuous $f\colon S^n\to\R^n$ satisfies $f(x)=f(-x)$ for some $x$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
For $n=1$, a map from connected $S^1$ to the two-point space $S^0$ is constant and cannot be odd. Take $n\ge2$ and use $\Z/2$ coefficients for the remainder of the homology argument.

Every singular simplex of $\R P^n$ has two lifts through $q:S^n\to\R P^n$, since its domain is convex and simply connected. Define the \emph{transfer} $\tau\sigma$ to be the sum of those two lifts. Faces lift in the same way, so $\tau$ is a chain map. We have a short exact sequence
\[
0\to C(\R P^n)\xrightarrow{\tau}C(S^n)\xrightarrow{q_\#}C(\R P^n)\to0.
\]
Indeed $q_\#$ is onto, $q_\#\tau=2=0$, and a chain maps to zero exactly when the coefficients of its two lifts over every simplex agree. Such chains are precisely transfer images. Distinct downstairs simplices have disjoint pairs of lifts, so $\tau$ is injective.

The zigzag lemma yields
\[
\cdots\to H_k(\R P^n)\xrightarrow{\tau_*}H_k(S^n)
\xrightarrow{q_*}H_k(\R P^n)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{k-1}(\R P^n)\to\cdots.
\]
The map $q_*$ on $H_0=\Z/2$ is the identity because both spaces are path-connected. Exactness then makes $\tau_*=0$ on $H_0$, so $\delta:H_1(\R P^n)\to H_0(\R P^n)$ is an isomorphism. In the remaining degrees $1<k<n$, the sphere terms on either side vanish, making $\delta$ an isomorphism again. Hence $H_k(\R P^n)=\Z/2$ for $0\le k<n$.

At the top the preceding lemma gives the exact segment
\[
0\to A\xrightarrow{\tau_*}\Z/2\xrightarrow{q_*}A
\xrightarrow{\delta}\Z/2\to0,\qquad A=H_n(\R P^n).
\]
The injection restricts $A$ to zero or $\Z/2$, while the final surjection rules out zero. Thus $A=\Z/2$, the transfer is an isomorphism, $q_*=0$, and $\delta$ is an isomorphism. These specific connecting and transfer maps are isomorphisms; the quotient map at the top is not.

If an odd $g:S^n\to S^{n-1}$ existed, include its target as the equator to obtain an odd self-map $f$ of $S^n$. It induces $\bar f$ on projective space. Oddness gives $f_\#\tau=\tau\bar f_\#$, because it carries each pair of antipodal lifts to the pair over the composed simplex. Naturality makes $\bar f_*$ commute with $\delta$. It is the identity on $H_0$, hence on every $H_k(\R P^n)$ through the connecting isomorphisms. The top transfer then makes $f_*$ an isomorphism on $H_n(S^n)$. But $f$ misses a point, so it factors through a contractible punctured sphere and has zero action there. This contradiction excludes $g$.

Finally, if $f(x)-f(-x)$ never vanished, its normalization would be an odd map to $S^{n-1}$. Conversely an odd map into $S^{n-1}\subset\R^n$ has distinct antipodal values, since its values are nonzero. This proves the equivalence.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
For $u=(u_0,u')\in S^n\subset\R\times\R^n$, put
\[
f_i(u)=\lambda\{x\in A_i:\langle u',x\rangle>u_0\}.
\]
When $u'\ne0$, the boundary hyperplane has measure zero, by a linear change of variables and Fubini. For convergent parameters its half-space indicator therefore converges almost everywhere; dominated convergence, with the integrable bound $1_{A_i}$, proves continuity. At $(1,0)$ the half-space misses all bounded $A_i$ for nearby parameters, and at $(-1,0)$ it contains them, so continuity holds there too.

Borsuk--Ulam gives $f_i(u)=f_i(-u)$ for every $i$. For $u'\ne0$ the two open half-spaces exhaust each $A_i$ up to a null hyperplane, so both measures equal $\lambda(A_i)/2$. If $u'=0$, equality forces every $A_i$ to be null, in which case any affine hyperplane works.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
(a) For scalars, the corresponding exponential and logarithmic power
series compose to the identity near zero. Comparing their convergent
series gives identities of coefficients. The same coefficients apply
to powers of a single matrix; absolute convergence in the operator norm
justifies the compositions and rearrangements.
In particular,
$\|e^X-I\|\le e^{\|X\|}-1<1$ for $\|X\|<\log2$.
The scalar identity $\log e^z=z$ on this neighbourhood therefore gives
$\log(e^X)=X$ as well.
(b) The tail is bounded by
\[
 \sum_{k\ge2}\frac{\|A-I\|^k}{k}
 \le\|A-I\|^2\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j}=2\|A-I\|^2.
\]
Thus $c=2$ works.
(c) The exponential series is smooth and
$e^X=I+X+O(\|X\|^2)$. Its differential at zero is the identity.
The inverse function theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse}, gives the local
diffeomorphism; part (a) identifies its inverse with this logarithm.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Choose $\varepsilon>0$ so that for $|t|\le\varepsilon$,
$\|\gamma(t)-I\|<1/2$ and $\|\log\gamma(t)\|<(\log2)/2$.
Set $X=(\log\gamma(\varepsilon))/\varepsilon$.
Let $B=\log\gamma(\varepsilon/2)$.
The homomorphism property gives
$e^{2B}=\gamma(\varepsilon)=e^{\varepsilon X}$.
Both exponents lie in the logarithm's inverse range, so $2B=\varepsilon X$.
Repeat the same argument at successive halves of $\varepsilon$.
It gives $\gamma(\varepsilon/2^k)=e^{\varepsilon X/2^k}$ for every $k$.
Taking positive and negative integer powers gives equality at every
$m\varepsilon/2^k$, $m\in\Z$. These points are dense in $\R$.
Continuity on both sides proves equality everywhere.
Differentiating the resulting exponential formula at zero gives
$X=\gamma'(0)$, proving uniqueness.

1_statement.original:
\label{prop:liealgebra}
For $X,Y\in M_n$, with $[X,Y]=XY-YX$,
\[e^{X+Y}=\lim_{m\to\infty}\bigl(e^{X/m}e^{Y/m}\bigr)^m\quad\text{(Lie's product formula)},\]
\[e^{[X,Y]}=\lim_{m\to\infty}\bigl(e^{X/m}e^{Y/m}e^{-X/m}e^{-Y/m}\bigr)^{m^2}.\]
Consequently the Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of a matrix Lie group is a real vector space closed under the bracket, and $gXg^{-1}\in\mathfrak g$ for $g\in G$, $X\in\mathfrak g$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
The first product is
$I+(X+Y)/m+O(m^{-2})$. Its logarithm is therefore
$Z_m=(X+Y)/m+O(m^{-2})$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:log}.
Its $m$th power is $e^{mZ_m}$, tending to $e^{X+Y}$.
For the second product, expand each exponential through degree two in
$s=1/m$. The first three factors give
\[
 e^{sX}e^{sY}e^{-sX}
 =I+sY+s^2([X,Y]+Y^2/2)+O(s^3).
\]
Multiplying by $e^{-sY}=I-sY+s^2Y^2/2+O(s^3)$ cancels the linear
term and both remaining $Y^2$ contributions. The product is therefore
$I+s^2[X,Y]+O(s^3)$. Its logarithm has the same leading term.
Multiplying that logarithm by $m^2$ gives $[X,Y]+O(m^{-1})$, proving
the second limit by continuity of the exponential.

If $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$, scalar multiples stay in $\mathfrak g$ by its
definition. Replace $X,Y$ by $tX,tY$ in the limits.
Every approximating product lies in $G$, and the limits are invertible,
so relative closedness in $GL_n$ gives
$e^{t(X+Y)}\in G$ and $e^{t^2[X,Y]}\in G$.
Interchanging $X,Y$ supplies the negative multiples of the bracket.
Thus every real multiple occurs, proving bracket closure.
Finally $e^{tgXg^{-1}}=ge^{tX}g^{-1}\in G$ proves conjugation invariance.

If $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$, scalar multiples stay in $\mathfrak g$ by its
definition. Replace $X,Y$ by $tX,tY$ in the limits.
Every approximating product lies in $G$, and the limits are invertible,
so relative closedness in $GL_n$ gives
$e^{t(X+Y)}\in G$ and $e^{t^2[X,Y]}\in G$.
Interchanging $X,Y$ supplies the negative multiples of the bracket.
Thus every real multiple occurs, proving bracket closure.
Finally $e^{tgXg^{-1}}=ge^{tX}g^{-1}\in G$ proves conjugation invariance.

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:closedsubgroup}
Suppose $G\subset GL_n$ is a matrix Lie group, and write $\mathfrak g$ for its Lie algebra.
There are neighbourhoods $U$ of $0$ in $M_n$ and $V$ of $I$ such that
$\exp:U\cap\mathfrak g\to V\cap G$ is a homeomorphism.
The group $G$ is a smooth submanifold of $M_n$, of dimension
$\dim\mathfrak g$, with $T_IG=\mathfrak g$. Multiplication and inversion
on $G$ are smooth.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Choose a vector-space complement $W$ to $\mathfrak g$ in $M_n$.
First show that for some $r>0$,
\[
 Y\in W,\quad0<\|Y\|<r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^Y\notin G.
\]
If no such $r$ existed, there would be nonzero $Y_m\in W$ tending to
zero with $e^{Y_m}\in G$. Passing to a subsequence on the compact unit
sphere gives $Y_m/\|Y_m\|\to Y\in W$ with $\|Y\|=1$.
For each fixed $t\in\R$, choose integers $k_m$ with
$k_m\|Y_m\|\to t$. Then
$e^{k_mY_m}=(e^{Y_m})^{k_m}\in G$ and $k_mY_m\to tY$.
Closedness gives $e^{tY}\in G$ for every $t$, hence
$Y\in\mathfrak g\cap W=\{0\}$, a contradiction.
If $W=\{0\}$ the assertion is vacuous and any $r$ works.

Consider $\Phi(X,Y)=e^Xe^Y$ on $\mathfrak g\times W$.
Its differential at $(0,0)$ is $(X,Y)\mapsto X+Y$, an isomorphism.
The inverse function theorem gives small product neighbourhoods
$U_{\mathfrak g}\times U_W$ on which $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism onto
an open set $V$ about $I$. Choose $U_W$ inside the radius-$r$ ball,
and $U_{\mathfrak g}$ inside a neighbourhood where $\exp$ is injective.
For $A=e^Xe^Y\in V$, if $A\in G$ then
$e^Y=e^{-X}A\in G$. Our first assertion forces $Y=0$.
Conversely $Y=0$ gives $A=e^X\in G$.
Thus in these coordinates
\[
 G\cap V=\Phi(U_{\mathfrak g}\times\{0\})=\exp(U_{\mathfrak g}).
\]
The coordinate slice is a submanifold, and its tangent space at $I$ is
$\mathfrak g$ because $d\exp_0$ is the identity.
Set $U=U_{\mathfrak g}+U_W$, an open neighbourhood in $M_n$.
Then $U\cap\mathfrak g=U_{\mathfrak g}$, giving the required
homeomorphism, in fact a diffeomorphism of these submanifolds.

Left multiplication by any $g\in G$ is an invertible linear map on
$M_n$ and carries this local description to a neighbourhood of $g$.
It follows that all of $G$ is a submanifold of the claimed dimension.
Matrix multiplication and inversion are smooth on $GL_n$;
their restrictions to this submanifold give smooth group operations.
The argument also includes $\mathfrak g=0$, when the local slice is a point.

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:homlie}
For a continuous homomorphism $\Phi:G\to H$ of matrix Lie groups there
is a unique real-linear map $\varphi:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak h$ with
$\Phi(e^X)=e^{\varphi(X)}$ for every $X\in\mathfrak g$.
It satisfies
\[
 \varphi([X,Y])=[\varphi(X),\varphi(Y)],\qquad
 \varphi(gXg^{-1})=\Phi(g)\varphi(X)\Phi(g)^{-1}.
\]
The map $\Phi$ is smooth and $\varphi=d\Phi_I$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
For each $X$, Proposition~\ref{prop:oneparameter} gives a unique
$\varphi(X)$ with $\Phi(e^{tX})=e^{t\varphi(X)}$ for all $t$.
These exponentials belong to $H$, so $\varphi(X)\in\mathfrak h$.
Rescaling the parameter gives $\varphi(sX)=s\varphi(X)$ for every real $s$.
The product formula and continuity give
\[
 e^{t\varphi(X+Y)}
 =\Phi\left(\lim_m(e^{tX/m}e^{tY/m})^m\right)
 =e^{t(\varphi(X)+\varphi(Y))}.
\]
Differentiate at $t=0$ to obtain additivity.
The commutator formula similarly gives
$e^{t^2\varphi([X,Y])}=e^{t^2[\varphi(X),\varphi(Y)]}$.
Comparing second derivatives at zero yields the bracket identity.
Conjugating the one-parameter subgroup by $g$ and applying $\Phi$
gives the second identity in the same way, by first derivatives at zero.

A real-linear map between finite-dimensional spaces is smooth.
In the exponential charts of Theorem~\ref{thm:closedsubgroup},
$\Phi=\exp\circ\varphi\circ\log$ near $I$, so $\Phi$ is smooth there.
The identity
$\Phi=L_{\Phi(g)}\circ\Phi\circ L_{g^{-1}}$ near $g$
then proves smoothness everywhere. Differentiating along $e^{tX}$ gives
$d\Phi_I(X)=\varphi(X)$. Any linear map with the displayed exponential
property has the same derivatives after replacing $X$ by $tX$,
which proves uniqueness.

1_statement.original:
\label{thm:spin}
The adjoint representation $\mathrm{Ad}\colon SU(2)\to GL(\mathfrak{su}(2))$, read in the basis $X(e_1),X(e_2),X(e_3)$, is a continuous surjective homomorphism $\pi\colon SU(2)\to SO(3)$ with kernel $\{\pm I\}$, and its differential is
the isomorphism $X(u)\mapsto L(u)$. It is a two-sheeted covering, and the universal covering of $SO(3)$. Consequently $SO(3)$ is homeomorphic to $\R P^3$ and
\[\pi_1(SO(3))\cong\Z/2.\]
The loop $\theta\mapsto e^{\theta L(u)}$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, of a full turn about an axis is not nullhomotopic, and the loop of two full turns is.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:spin}
In the basis $X(e_1),X(e_2),X(e_3)$, the adjoint representation of
$SU(2)$ is a continuous surjective homomorphism
$\pi:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ with kernel $\{I,-I\}$.
Its differential is the isomorphism $X(u)\mapsto L(u)$.
It is a two-sheeted universal covering. In particular,
$SO(3)\cong\R P^3$ as topological spaces and
$\pi_1(SO(3))\cong\Z/2$.
For each unit vector $u$, the full-turn loop
$\theta\mapsto e^{\theta L(u)}$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$,
is not nullhomotopic, while the loop of two full turns is nullhomotopic.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
\emph{The image consists of rotations.}
The real inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-2\operatorname{tr}(XY)$
makes the displayed basis orthonormal, since
$\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}$.
Conjugation preserves this inner product by cyclicity of trace.
Thus $\pi(g)$ is orthogonal. Its determinant is a continuous function
from connected $S^3$ to $\{1,-1\}$, equal to one at $I$;
it is therefore always one.

\emph{The differential and surjectivity.}
The differential is $\mathrm{ad}$, and
$\mathrm{ad}_{X(u)}X(v)=X(u\times v)$ represents $L(u)$.
Hence $\pi(e^{X(u)})=e^{L(u)}$.
Every spatial rotation has this exponential form, so $\pi$ is onto.

\emph{The kernel and covering.}
If $\pi(g)=I$, then $g$ commutes with all $X(u)$ and hence with all
Pauli matrices. Together with $I$ these span $M_2(\C)$, so $g$ is
scalar. Its determinant is one, forcing $g=I$ or $-I$.
Both do lie in the kernel.
The resulting map $S^3/\{\pm1\}\to SO(3)$ is a continuous bijection
from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism.
The source is $\R P^3$, and $S^3\to\R P^3$ is the two-sheeted
covering of Example~\ref{ex:coverings}(d).
Since $S^3$ is simply connected by Corollary~\ref{cor:spheres}, this
is the universal covering. The covering-space calculation from
Example~\ref{ex:computations}(b) gives fundamental group $\Z/2$.

\emph{Lift a turn.}
Let $|u|=1$. Since $X(u)^2=-I/4$, separating even and odd powers gives
\[
 e^{\theta X(u)}=\cos(\theta/2)I+2\sin(\theta/2)X(u).
\]
This is the lift starting at $I$ of $e^{\theta L(u)}$.
At $\theta=2\pi$ it equals $-I$, so the lift is not closed.
A nullhomotopic loop would have a closed lift, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:fibre}; the full turn is therefore not nullhomotopic.
At $4\pi$ the lift returns to $I$. Its closed loop contracts in $S^3$,
and projection of that contraction contracts the two-turn loop in $SO(3)$.

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:torus}
Let $T\subset U(n)$ be the diagonal unitary subgroup, isomorphic to
$(S^1)^n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Each element of $U(n)$ is conjugate by a unitary matrix to an
element of $T$. The exponential $\mathfrak u(n)\to U(n)$ is onto and
$U(n)$ is connected.
\item[(b)] If $t\in T$ has distinct diagonal entries, its centraliser in
$U(n)$ is exactly $T$. Consequently $T$ is maximal abelian.
\item[(c)] Its normaliser $N(T)=\{g\in U(n):gTg^{-1}=T\}$ consists
of the matrices $P_wD$, where $D\in T$ and $P_w$ is a permutation
matrix. The quotient $N(T)/T$ is $S_n$, acting by permuting diagonal entries.
\item[(d)] Two elements of $T$ are conjugate in $U(n)$ exactly when their
diagonal entries agree after a permutation.
\end{enumerate}

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
(a) A unitary matrix is normal. The spectral theorem
(Volume~8, Theorem~3.2) writes it as
$g=U\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta_j})U^*$.
Then $g=e^X$ with $X=U\operatorname{diag}(i\theta_j)U^*\in\mathfrak u(n)$,
and $s\mapsto e^{sX}$ joins $I$ to $g$.
(b) A matrix commuting with $t$ preserves each of its one-dimensional
coordinate eigenspaces. It is diagonal, and if unitary belongs to $T$.
Conversely all elements of $T$ commute. Any abelian subgroup containing
$T$ must commute with this particular $t$, so it cannot be larger.
(c) For $g\in N(T)$, the diagonal matrix $gtg^{-1}$ has the same
set of distinct eigenvalues as $t$. Some permutation $w$ gives
$gtg^{-1}=P_wtP_w^{-1}$. Thus $P_w^{-1}g$ commutes with $t$
and belongs to $T$, proving $g=P_wD$.
Conversely each such matrix normalises all diagonal matrices.
Its permutation of coordinate lines is unique, and composition composes
these permutations. This gives a homomorphism onto $S_n$ with kernel $T$.
(d) Conjugation preserves eigenvalues with multiplicity. Conversely
permutation matrices realise every permutation, including when entries repeat.

1_statement.original:
\label{thm:haarform}
Let $\omega_I$ be a non-zero alternating $m$-form on $\mathfrak g$. The formula
\[\omega_g(gX_1,\dots,gX_m)=\omega_I(X_1,\dots,X_m)\qquad(X_i\in\mathfrak g)\]
defines a smooth nowhere vanishing $m$-form on $G$ with $L_h^*\omega=\omega$ for all $h$, and $\mu=|\omega|$ is a left Haar measure on $G$. Moreover
\[R_h^*\omega=\det\bigl(\mathrm{Ad}(h^{-1})\bigr)\,\omega,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\mu(Eh)=\bigl|\det\mathrm{Ad}(h^{-1})\bigr|\,\mu(E),\]
where $\mathrm{Ad}(h)\colon\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$ is the linear map $X\mapsto hXh^{-1}$.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:haarform}
Choose a nonzero alternating $m$-form $\omega_I$ on $\mathfrak g$.
The rule
\[
 \omega_g(gX_1,\ldots,gX_m)=\omega_I(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
\]
defines a smooth nowhere-zero form on $G$ satisfying $L_h^*\omega=\omega$.
Its measure $\mu=|\omega|$ is a left Haar measure.
Moreover, for every $h\in G$ and Borel set $E$,
\[
 R_h^*\omega=\det(\mathrm{Ad}(h^{-1}))\,\omega,\qquad
 \mu(Eh)=|\det\mathrm{Ad}(h^{-1})|\,\mu(E).
\]
Here $\mathrm{Ad}(h)X=hXh^{-1}$ acts on $\mathfrak g$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Choose a basis $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ of $\mathfrak g$ and extend its dual
coordinate forms to linear functionals $\ell_i$ on $M_n$.
The forms $\theta^i_g(v)=\ell_i(g^{-1}v)$ are smooth on $GL_n$.
Restricted to $G$, they form the dual frame to $gX_1,\ldots,gX_m$.
Thus
$\omega=c\,\theta^1\wedge\cdots\wedge\theta^m$,
where $c=\omega_I(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\ne0$.
This proves smoothness and nonvanishing, and also supplies an orientation
on every component. For $m=0$ the empty wedge is one and $\omega=c$
on the discrete group, so the same construction gives $|c|$ times counting
measure.

The differential of $L_h$ sends $gX_i$ to $hgX_i$.
Evaluating the definition on this basis proves $L_h^*\omega=\omega$.
Change of variables then gives $\mu(hE)=\mu(E)$.
In charts the measure has a continuous strictly positive density.
A compact set is covered by finitely many small chart neighbourhoods
with bounded densities and bounded coordinate volumes, so has finite
measure. Every nonempty open set contains a chart ball of positive
measure. Local Lebesgue regularity and a countable atlas give regularity
of the measure. These are the Haar measure properties.

For right translation, its differential sends $gX_i$ to
$gX_ih=gh(h^{-1}X_ih)$. Therefore
\[
 (R_h^*\omega)_g(gX_1,\ldots,gX_m)
 =\omega_I(\mathrm{Ad}(h^{-1})X_1,\ldots,
             \mathrm{Ad}(h^{-1})X_m).
\]
Alternating top forms multiply by the determinant of the applied linear
map, proving the form identity. Taking its absolute measure and applying
change of variables to $\mathbf1_{Eh}$ gives the stated right-translation
factor. In dimension zero this determinant is the empty determinant one.

\label{cor:compactunimodular}
If $G$ is compact, then $\delta=1$: the measure $\mu$ is also right invariant. If $G$ is compact and connected, $R_h^*\omega=\omega$ for every $h$.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{cor:compactunimodular}
On a compact matrix Lie group, $\delta(h)=1$ for every $h$, so its Haar
measure is also right invariant. If the group is compact and connected,
then its left-invariant volume form itself satisfies $R_h^*\omega=\omega$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
The map $h\mapsto\det\mathrm{Ad}(h^{-1})$ is a continuous homomorphism
into $\R^\times$. Its image is compact. An element of absolute value
different from one would have unbounded positive or negative integer
powers, so every image value is $1$ or $-1$.
Their absolute values are one, proving the measure statement.
For a connected group the image is connected and contains one, so it
consists only of one, proving the stronger form statement.

1_statement.original:
\label{thm:haarcompact}
Let $G$ be a compact metrizable group carrying a right invariant Borel probability $\mu$. Every left invariant finite Borel measure $\nu$ on $G$ equals $\nu(G)\mu$.
In particular, on a compact matrix Lie group there is exactly one left invariant Borel probability, the Haar measure $\mu$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:haarform}; it is right
invariant, and invariant under inversion: $\mu(E^{-1})=\mu(E)$.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:haarcompact}
Suppose a compact metrizable group $G$ carries a right-invariant Borel
probability $\mu$. Every finite left-invariant Borel measure $\nu$ then
satisfies $\nu=\nu(G)\mu$.
In particular, a compact matrix Lie group has exactly one left-invariant
Borel probability. It is the normalised measure above, is right invariant,
and satisfies $\mu(E^{-1})=\mu(E)$ for every Borel $E$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
For continuous $f$, apply Fubini to $f(yx)$ with measures $\nu(x)$ and
$\mu(y)$. Left invariance of $\nu$ makes its integral in $x$ equal to
$\int f\,\dd\nu$ for every $y$. Right invariance of $\mu$ makes its
integral in $y$ equal to $\int f\,\dd\mu$ for every $x$.
Consequently
\[
 \int f\,\dd\nu
 =\int_G\int_Gf(yx)\,\dd\nu(x)\,\dd\mu(y)
 =\nu(G)\int f\,\dd\mu.
\]
Finite Borel measures on a compact metric space are determined by these
continuous-function integrals. Explicitly, for a nonempty compact $K$, the continuous
functions $\max(0,1-jd(x,K))$ decrease to $\mathbf1_K$.
Dominated convergence gives equality on compact sets, and Borel regularity
gives equality on all Borel sets, as in Volume~8, Theorem~13.3.

For compact matrix groups, the preceding corollary makes the constructed
probability right invariant, so the uniqueness result applies to it.
The measure $\check\mu(E)=\mu(E^{-1})$ is another left-invariant
probability: $(hE)^{-1}=E^{-1}h^{-1}$ and $\mu$ is right invariant.
Uniqueness gives $\check\mu=\mu$.

1_statement.original:
\label{ex:su2haar}
A matrix of $SU(2)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a&-\bar b\\b&\bar a\end{pmatrix}$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$, and is determined by its first column; this identifies $SU(2)$ with the unit sphere
$S^3\subset\C^2=\R^4$. Under this identification, left multiplication by $g\in SU(2)$ is the map $z\mapsto gz$ on first columns, which is unitary, hence an orthogonal map of $\R^4$.
The uniform probability $\sigma_3$ on $S^3$ is the law of $Z/|Z|$ for a standard Gaussian vector $Z$ in $\R^4$ (polar coordinates, as in the solution of Exercise~\ref{ex:spherevolume}), and
the Gaussian law is invariant under orthogonal maps. So $\sigma_3$ is a left invariant probability on $SU(2)$: \emph{the Haar measure of $SU(2)$ is the uniform measure on $S^3$.}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:pushhaar} and the double cover $SU(2)\to SO(3)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}, a Haar random rotation is obtained by taking a uniform point of $S^3$, a unit
quaternion, and the rotation it induces. This is how computer graphics draws random orientations (Ken Shoemake's method of 1992), and Exercise~\ref{ex:su2weyl} computes
how large the angle of a random rotation is.
1_statement.reviewed:
\label{ex:su2haar}
The first column identifies $SU(2)$ with
$S^3=\{(a,b)\in\C^2:|a|^2+|b|^2=1\}$.
Left multiplication by $g\in SU(2)$ acts on that column by the unitary
map $z\mapsto gz$, hence by an orthogonal map of $\R^4$.
For a standard real Gaussian vector $Z\in\R^4$, polar coordinates show
that $Z/|Z|$ has uniform spherical probability, as in
Exercise~\ref{ex:spherevolume}. The zero vector has probability zero.
The Gaussian law and the spherical probability are invariant under all
orthogonal maps, so this spherical law is left invariant on $SU(2)$.
Uniqueness makes it Haar probability.

Push it through the spin covering of Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}.
A uniform unit quaternion therefore produces a Haar random spatial
rotation. This is the basis of Shoemake's random-orientation construction.
It does not mean choosing the rotation angle uniformly: the angle density
will be computed in Exercise~\ref{ex:su2weyl}.

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{lem:qr}
Each invertible complex matrix $Z$ has a unique factorisation $Z=QR$,
where $Q$ is unitary and $R$ is upper triangular with strictly positive
real diagonal. The map $Z\mapsto Q$ is continuous on $GL_n(\C)$.
A matrix with independent standard complex Gaussian entries is invertible
with probability one.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Apply Gram--Schmidt to the columns. At step $k$, subtract the projections
on the earlier orthonormal columns and divide the remaining vector by its
positive norm. Linear independence makes that norm nonzero.
This gives $Z=QR$ with the required diagonal and gives continuous formulas
for all columns of $Q$ on $GL_n$.
If $QR=Q'R'$, then $Q'^{-1}Q=R'R^{-1}$ is both unitary and upper
triangular with positive diagonal. Its first column has just its first
entry; norm one and orthogonality force the other first-row entries to
vanish. Repeat on the lower block. The matrix is diagonal with unit-modulus
positive entries, hence the identity. This proves uniqueness.

For Gaussian columns, condition on the first $k-1$ columns.
Their complex span is a proper real linear subspace of $\C^n$ when
$k\le n$, and has Lebesgue measure zero. The independent $k$th column
has a density, so it lies in that span with probability zero.
Fubini and the finitely many steps prove almost-sure independence.

4_proof_steps.reviewed_proof:
\emph{Remove the singular matrices.}
The Jacobian lemma says that $\Phi$ is critical exactly on
$\mathcal O\times T_{\mathrm{sing}}$, and its image there is precisely
$U(n)_{\mathrm{sing}}$.
Sard's theorem in equal dimensions, Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}, applied in
countably many charts, makes this image null in every target chart.
Haar measure has a continuous density there, so its measure is zero.
The set $T_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is a finite union of diagonal subtori
$t_j=t_k$ and has zero torus volume. For $n=1$ both singular sets are empty.

\emph{Count every regular preimage.}
On the regular set the Jacobian is nonzero, so $\Phi$ is a local
diffeomorphism with exactly $n!$ sheets by Lemma~\ref{lem:sheets}.
Its image is $U(n)_{\mathrm{reg}}$, which is therefore open.
For a Borel set $E$ inside one evenly covered neighbourhood, change of
variables on each sheet gives
\[
 \int_{\mathcal O\times T_{\mathrm{reg}}}
       \mathbf1_E\circ\Phi\,\dd|\Phi^*\omega|=n!\mu(E).
\]
A countable base gives a countable cover by such neighbourhoods.
Cut any Borel set into disjoint pieces, each inside one of them, and add.
Then pass from indicators to bounded Borel functions.
The singular sets just removed contribute zero, so
\[
 \int_{\mathcal O\times T}f\circ\Phi\,\dd|\Phi^*\omega|
 =n!\int_{U(n)}f\,\dd\mu.
\]
This measure identity uses the absolute Jacobian, hence $|C|$, irrespective
of the orientation signs of the chosen forms.

\emph{Integrate out the eigenlines and normalise.}
For a class function, $f(\Phi(H,t))=f(t)$.
The Jacobian and product-measure rules give
\[
 n!\int f\,\dd\mu
 =|C|\left(\int_{\mathcal O}\dd|\sigma|\right)
       \int_Tf(t)|V(t)|^2\,\dd\theta.
\]
The coefficient is positive and independent of $f$.
Expand both Vandermonde determinants:
\[
 |V(t)|^2=\sum_{\pi,\rho\in S_n}
 \operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)
 \prod_ke^{i(\pi(k)-\rho(k))\theta_k}.
\]
Circle integration kills a term unless $\pi(k)=\rho(k)$ for every $k$.
Exactly $n!$ terms survive, each with integral $(2\pi)^n$.
Since $\mu(U(n))=1$, setting $f=1$ determines the coefficient as
$1/(n!(2\pi)^n)$, proving the formula.
For randomly ordered eigenvalues, average any test function over all
permutations. This symmetric test is a class function; the density is
symmetric too. The formula therefore gives the asserted joint law.

\label{lem:orbit}
For $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,n)$, the orbit
$\mathcal O=\{gDg^{-1}:g\in U(n)\}$ is a compact submanifold of
$\mathrm{Herm}_n$ of dimension $n^2-n$.
Its tangent space at $D$ consists of the zero-diagonal Hermitian matrices.
There is a smooth nowhere-zero $(n^2-n)$-form $\sigma$ on $\mathcal O$
with $c_g^*\sigma=\sigma$ for every $g\in U(n)$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Set $p(H)=(\operatorname{tr}H,\ldots,\operatorname{tr}H^n)$.
The first $n$ power sums of eigenvalues determine the characteristic
polynomial by Newton's identities
\[
 ke_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i,\qquad e_0=1.
\]
These follow by differentiating
$E(x)=\prod_j(1+\lambda_jx)=\sum_ke_kx^k$ and comparing coefficients
in $xE'(x)=E(x)\sum_{i\ge1}(-1)^{i-1}p_ix^i$.
The spectral theorem therefore gives $p^{-1}(p(D))=\mathcal O$.
The orbit is compact as the continuous image of compact $U(n)$.

Differentiation and cyclicity of trace give
$dp_H(K)=(k\operatorname{tr}(H^{k-1}K))_{1\le k\le n}$.
At $H=gDg^{-1}$, its values on $gE_{jj}g^{-1}$ are the vectors
$(kj^{k-1})_k$. The matrix with these columns is a Vandermonde matrix
times an invertible diagonal matrix, so they are independent.
Thus $p(D)$ is a regular value. The regular value theorem gives the
claimed dimension and tangent space $\ker dp_H$.
At $D$, the same Vandermonde invertibility says that the kernel condition
is exactly $K_{jj}=0$ for every $j$.

The normal vectors $N_k(H)=kH^{k-1}$ are the gradients of $p_k$.
They are independent and span the orthogonal complement of the tangent
space. Define
\[
 \sigma_H(K_1,\ldots,K_{n^2-n})
 =\mathrm{vol}(N_1(H),\ldots,N_n(H),K_1,\ldots,K_{n^2-n}).
\]
This is smooth and nonzero on every tangent basis.
Since $N_k(c_gH)=c_gN_k(H)$ and $c_g$ preserves the ambient volume,
it preserves $\sigma$. For $n=1$ the orbit is a point and this construction
is a nonzero zero-form, consistent with the stated dimension.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
Write $\Phi^*\omega=J(H,t)\,\sigma\wedge\dd\theta$.
Conjugation on $U(n)$ preserves $\omega$, since it is a left translation
followed by a right translation and the group is compact and connected.
The identity $\Phi(c_gH,t)=c_g\Phi(H,t)$ and invariance of $\sigma$
give $J(c_gH,t)=J(H,t)$. It is enough to compute at $H=D$.

A tangent vector there is $(K,it\Theta)$, with $K$ Hermitian of zero
diagonal and $\Theta$ real diagonal. Put $X_{jj}=0$ and
$X_{jk}=K_{jk}/(k-j)$ for $j\ne k$.
Then $X^*=-X$ and $[X,D]=K$.
Differentiate the curve $(e^{sX}De^{-sX},te^{is\Theta})$ under $\Phi$.
Its image has derivative
\[
 Xt-tX+it\Theta=t(t^{-1}Xt-X+i\Theta).
\]
Left invariance lets us remove the factor $t$ when evaluating $\omega$.
Use the complex coordinates $K_{jk}$, $j<k$, and real diagonal coordinates
$\Theta_{jj}$ on the source tangent space.
On the target algebra, use its upper-diagonal complex entries and diagonal
entries divided by $i$. The derivative fixes each $\Theta_{jj}$ and
multiplies each $K_{jk}$ by
\[
 z_{jk}=\frac{t_k/t_j-1}{k-j}.
\]
Multiplication by a complex number $z$ has real determinant $|z|^2$.
The full determinant is therefore
\[
 \prod_{j<k}\frac{|t_k-t_j|^2}{(k-j)^2}.
\]
The fixed ratios of our coordinate volume forms contribute a nonzero
constant independent of $t$. This proves the formula, including its zeros
when eigenvalues coincide.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
(a) If $\Phi(H,t)=gtg^{-1}$, its eigenvalues are precisely the entries
of $t$, proving the inverse-image assertion.
For a regular matrix, assign the labels $1,\ldots,n$ to its distinct
eigenlines in any order. This determines $H$ uniquely, with label $j$
as its eigenvalue on the assigned line, and determines $t_j$ as the
unitary eigenvalue on that line. Each of the $n!$ assignments works and
no others do.
(b) For $N=0$ the source is empty and the assertion is vacuous.
Otherwise write $F^{-1}(y)=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}$ and choose disjoint
local inverse neighbourhoods at these points.
Intersect their image neighbourhoods to obtain an open $W$ about $y$.
Every point of $W$ already has one preimage in each branch.
It cannot have an additional preimage outside them, since its fibre has
exactly $N$ points. Restricting those branches over $W$ therefore gives
the whole inverse image and the required disjoint covering.

Expand the determinant as a sum over $\pi\in S_m$.
Terms with $\pi(m)=m$ have a factor $K(x_m,x_m)$ integrating to $c$.

In every other term, the cycle containing $m$ has a predecessor $j<m$

$K(x_j,x_m)K(x_m,x_l)$, which integrate to $K(x_j,x_l)$.
Removing $m$ from that cycle reverses its permutation sign.
Each permutation on $m-1$ symbols arises exactly $m-1$ times: insert

first contribution exists, giving $c$ as required.

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:correlations}
Let the eigenangles of a Haar $U\in U(n)$ be
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n\in[0,2\pi)$.
For $1\le k\le n$ and every bounded Borel function $g$ on $[0,2\pi)^k$,
\[
 \mathbb E\sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_k\ \mathrm{distinct}}
       g(\theta_{j_1},\ldots,\theta_{j_k})
 =\int g(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_k)
       \det(K_n(\varphi_a,\varphi_b))_{a,b\le k}
       \frac{\dd\varphi_1\cdots\dd\varphi_k}{(2\pi)^k}.
\]
The sum is over ordered tuples of distinct indices and is independent
of the ordering chosen for the eigenangles.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
For $A=(e^{ij\theta_l})_{0\le j<n,\ 1\le l\le n}$,
the Gram determinant identity gives
\[
 |V|^2=|\det A|^2=\det(A^*A)
       =\det(K_n(\theta_a,\theta_b))_{a,b\le n}.
\]
The last matrix may be transposed relative to $A^*A$; transposition does
not change its determinant.
Use the randomly ordered joint law from Weyl's theorem.
Its symmetry makes all $n!/(n-k)!$ terms of the sum contribute the same
integral. The expectation is therefore
\[
 \frac1{(n-k)!}\int g(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k)
       \det(K_n(\theta_a,\theta_b))_{a,b\le n}
       \frac{\dd\theta_1\cdots\dd\theta_n}{(2\pi)^n}.
\]
The kernel satisfies Gaudin's assumptions with $c=n$, by the orthogonality
identities above. Integrating out $\theta_n,\ldots,\theta_{k+1}$
produces factors $1,2,\ldots,n-k$.
They cancel the factorial, giving the result. For $k=n$ there are no
integrations to perform and the factorial is $0!=1$.

1_statement.original:
\label{cor:dyson}
For $x\in\R$ let $\langle x\rangle\in(-\pi,\pi]$ be the representative of $x$ modulo $2\pi$. For every continuous $h$ with compact support on $\R$,
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\,\mathbb E\sum_{j\neq k}h\Bigl(\frac n{2\pi}\langle\theta_j-\theta_k\rangle\Bigr)=\int_{\R}h(u)\Bigl(1-\Bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\Bigr)^2\Bigr)\dd u.\]
For $n$ independent uniform points in place of the eigenvalues, the limit is $\int h(u)\dd u$.

\label{cor:dyson}
For real $x$, let $\langle x\rangle\in(-\pi,\pi]$ be its representative

\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\sum_{j\ne k}
 h\left(\frac n{2\pi}\langle\theta_j-\theta_k\rangle\right)
 =\int_\R h(u)\left[1-\left(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\right)^2\right]\dd u.
\]

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
For $n\ge2$, apply the two-point correlation formula.
Its integrand depends only on the circular difference
$x=\langle\varphi_1-\varphi_2\rangle$.
For fixed $\varphi_2$, this difference preserves uniform circle measure.
The expectation divided by $n$ becomes
\[
 \frac1n\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}h\left(\frac{nx}{2\pi}\right)
 \left[n^2-\frac{\sin^2(nx/2)}{\sin^2(x/2)}\right]\frac{\dd x}{2\pi}.
\]
Set $x=2\pi u/n$. The result is
\[
 \int_{-n/2}^{n/2}h(u)
 \left[1-\frac{\sin^2\pi u}{n^2\sin^2(\pi u/n)}\right]\dd u.
\]
The bracket lies in $[0,1]$ because $|K_n|\le n$.
At $u=0$ it has continuous value zero.
For fixed $u\ne0$, $n\sin(\pi u/n)\to\pi u$, giving the limiting
bracket; at zero the same limit holds by the convention just stated.
For all sufficiently large $n$ the integration interval contains the
support of $h$. The absolute integrand is bounded by $|h(u)|$,
which is integrable. Dominated convergence applies even when $h$ has
negative or complex values and proves the limit.

For independent points, each ordered pair has uniform circular difference.
The same substitution gives
$(n-1)n^{-1}\int_{-n/2}^{n/2}h(u)\,\dd u$, tending to $\int h$.
No assertion for a two-point correlation at $n=1$ is needed for either limit.

The \emph{hyperbolic length} of a piecewise $C^1$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb H$ is $L(\gamma)=\int_0^1\frac{|\gamma'(t)|}{\operatorname{Im}\gamma(t)}\,dt$.
The \emph{hyperbolic distance} $d(z,w)$ is the infimum of $L(\gamma)$ over the paths from $z$ to $w$. The \emph{hyperbolic area} of a region $R$ is
$\iint_R\frac{dx\,dy}{y^2}$.

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{geometry:prop:isometries}
If $a,b,c,d$ are real and $ad-bc=1$, the map $g(z)=(az+b)/(cz+d)$ is a bijection of $\mathbb H$ preserving hyperbolic lengths, distances and areas. The reflection $z\mapsto-\bar z$ has the same preservation properties.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
The denominator cannot vanish in $\mathbb H$: when $c\ne0$ its zero is real, and when $c=0$ the determinant condition gives $d\ne0$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $c\bar z+d$ gives
\[
\operatorname{Im}g(z)=\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{|cz+d|^2},
\qquad g'(z)=\frac1{(cz+d)^2}.
\]
The first expression is positive. The inverse comes from the real determinant-one matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and also maps $\mathbb H$ into itself, so $g$ is onto. For every path, the factor $|c\gamma+d|^{-2}$ occurs in both $|(g\circ\gamma)'|$ and $\operatorname{Im}(g\circ\gamma)$, and cancels in the length integral. Applying the inverse shows that the two sets of path lengths, hence their infima, agree. For area, the absolute Jacobian is $|g'|^2=|cz+d|^{-4}$; this cancels the change in the factor $y^{-2}$. Reflection keeps $y$ and $|dz|$ fixed and has absolute Jacobian $1$.

Two distinct points $z,w\in\mathbb H$ lie on exactly one h-line. A transformation from Proposition~\ref{geometry:prop:isometries} sends that line to the imaginary axis and sends $z,w$ to $i,it$, respectively, for some $t>1$.

\[

\]
The circle with this centre through $z$ also contains $w$.

Divide the image by $s$. If $s'/s<1$, apply $J$, which fixes $i$ and replaces $i(s'/s)$ by $i(s/s')$.

Start with $i,it$, where $t>1$. Write a joining path as $x(s)+iy(s)$. Then
\[
L(\gamma)\ge\int_0^1\frac{|y'(s)|}{y(s)}\,ds
\ge\int_0^1\frac{y'(s)}{y(s)}\,ds=\log t.
\]
The first inequality is an equality precisely when $x'=0$ on each smooth piece; the second requires $y'\ge0$. Thus only the upward vertical segment can minimize length, and its length is $\log t$. The proposed formula gives
$1+(t-1)^2/(2t)=(t+t^{-1})/2=\cosh(\log t)$.

\[
g(z)-g(w)=\frac{z-w}{(cz+d)(cw+d)},
\qquad \operatorname{Im}g(z)=\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{|cz+d|^2}.
\]
The denominator factors cancel. H-lines and minimizing paths map to h-lines and minimizing paths, so uniqueness follows from the vertical case. If $z=w$, both sides of the formula are $1$; a path has length zero only when it is constant.

\[

\label{geometry:thm:hyparea}
A hyperbolic triangle with angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ has area $\pi-\alpha-\beta-\gamma$.

\label{geometry:thm:hyparea}

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
First suppose that one vertex is ideal. Move it to $\infty$; the two sides ending there become vertical lines. Translate and dilate so that the circle carrying the third side is the unit circle. The region is
\[
x_0\le x\le x_1,\qquad y\ge\sqrt{1-x^2}.
\]
Angles between tangents equal angles between their perpendiculars. Thus, with left and right angles $\alpha,\beta$, its lower endpoints have $x_0=\cos(\pi-\alpha)$ and $x_1=\cos\beta$. Integrating first in $y$ gives
\[
\operatorname{area}=\int_{x_0}^{x_1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
=\arccos x_0-\arccos x_1=\pi-\alpha-\beta.
\]
An ideal endpoint of the lower arc gives $x_0=-1$ or $x_1=1$. The same convergent improper integral covers triangles with two or three ideal vertices.

For a triangle $ABC$ with finite vertices, extend the side from $A$ through $C$ to an ideal point $D$. The larger triangle $ABD$ consists of $ABC$ and $CBD$, sharing only $BC$. Denote the angle of $CBD$ at $B$ by $\delta$. The angle of $ABD$ there is $\beta+\delta$, while the angle of $CBD$ at $C$ is $\pi-\gamma$. Applying the ideal-vertex case twice and subtracting gives
\[
\operatorname{area}(ABC)
=[\pi-\alpha-\beta-\delta]-[\pi-(\pi-\gamma)-\delta]
=\pi-\alpha-\beta-\gamma.
\]

\]

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:trace}
Let $g\in SL_2(\R)$ with $g\ne\pm I$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $|\operatorname{tr}g|<2$, then $g$ has exactly one fixed point $z_0\in\mathbb H$ and is conjugate to some $k_\theta$. It is a rotation about $z_0$, called \emph{elliptic}.
\item[(b)] If $|\operatorname{tr}g|=2$, then $g$ has no fixed point in $\mathbb H$ and exactly one in $\R\cup\{\infty\}$. It is conjugate to $\pm n_1$ or $\pm n_{-1}$ and is called \emph{parabolic}.
\item[(c)] If $|\operatorname{tr}g|>2$, then $g$ is conjugate to $\pm\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})$, where $\lambda>1$, and is called \emph{hyperbolic}. It fixes two boundary points and translates their joining h-line, its \emph{axis}, by $\ell=2\log\lambda$. For every $z\in\mathbb H$,
\[
d(z,g(z))\ge\ell,
\qquad 2\cosh(\ell/2)=|\operatorname{tr}g|,
\]
with equality in the distance inequality exactly on the axis.
\end{enumerate}

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
A finite fixed point satisfies $cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$. Its discriminant is $(a+d)^2-4$, so the trace divides the argument into three cases.

If its absolute value is less than $2$, then $c\ne0$: otherwise $ad=1$ would give $|a+d|\ge2$. The two roots are conjugate and nonreal, exactly one in $\mathbb H$. Move that root to $i$ by conjugation. The conjugated matrix fixes $i$, so the Iwasawa theorem puts it in $K$.

If the absolute trace exceeds $2$, the matrix has two distinct real eigenvalues. After replacing $g$ by $-g$ if necessary, order them as $\lambda,\lambda^{-1}$ with $\lambda>1$. Choose eigenvectors in this order, change the sign of one if needed, and scale the resulting basis matrix to have determinant $1$. In that basis the transformation is $z\mapsto\lambda^2z$. It fixes $0,\infty$ and moves the imaginary axis a distance $2\log\lambda$. For $z=x+iy$,
\[
\cosh d(z,\lambda^2z)
=1+\frac{(\lambda^2-1)^2(x^2+y^2)}{2\lambda^2y^2}
\ge\frac{\lambda^2+\lambda^{-2}}2
=\cosh(2\log\lambda).
\]
Equality holds exactly when $x=0$. Conjugation preserves distances and sends this axis to the axis of $g$. The trace identity follows from $\lambda+\lambda^{-1}=2\cosh(\log\lambda)$.

Finally, absolute trace $2$ gives a repeated eigenvalue $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. Since $g\ne\varepsilon I$, choose a real eigenvector $v$ and complete it to an oriented determinant-one basis $(v,w)$. In this basis $g=\varepsilon\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&u\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with $u\ne0$. Conjugating by $a_t$ replaces $u$ by $e^tu$, so its magnitude can be made $1$. Translation by $1$ or $-1$ fixes only $\infty$ on the boundary and no point in $\mathbb H$.

4_proof_steps.direct_following_proof:
For (a), a matrix with integral inverse takes primitive integer column vectors to primitive vectors. Applying it to the two endpoint columns multiplies their determinant by $\pm1$, preserving the neighbour condition. A determinant-minus-one transformation is reflection $z\mapsto-\bar z$ followed by the determinant-one matrix obtained by negating its first column. It is therefore an isometry. If $ps-qr=1$, the matrix with columns $(p,q)^T,(r,s)^T$ sends $\infty,0$ to the chosen endpoints. Interchange the endpoint columns when the determinant is $-1$. This proves transitivity for unoriented edges.

For (b), two distinct h-lines cross exactly when their endpoints alternate around the boundary circle. This follows directly for a vertical axis, whose opposite sides are the positive and negative real half-lines, and then for every h-line by an isometry. Send one proposed crossing edge to $(0,\infty)$. The other would have finite endpoints $p/q<0<r/s$, with $p<0<r$ and $q,s\ge1$. But then
\[
|ps-qr|=|p|s+qr\ge2,
\]
contradicting the Farey condition.

For (c), a distinct edge entering $\Delta_0$ could not cross any of its three sides, by (b). It would have to remain there in both directions. The closure of this triangle meets the boundary only at $0,1,\infty$, so the edge would have to join two of these vertices and hence be a side, a contradiction. Part (a) transports this argument to every image. Finally
\[
g=\begin{pmatrix}r&p\\s&q\end{pmatrix}\in SL_2(\Z)
\]
sends $0,\infty$ to $p/q,r/s$. The triangles $\Delta_0$ and $\Delta_0-1$ share $(0,\infty)$ and have third vertices $1,-1$. Their images have the claimed third vertices, since $g(1)=(p+r)/(q+s)$ and $g(-1)=(r-p)/(s-q)$.

1_statement.reviewed:
\label{thm:cutting}
Let $x>1$ be irrational, with continued fraction $x=[a_0;a_1,a_2,\ldots]$, and let $-1<y<0$. After crossing the edge $(0,\infty)$, the h-line from $y$ to $x$ has cutting sequence
\[
L^{a_0}R^{a_1}L^{a_2}R^{a_3}\cdots.
\]
1_statement.comparison: Compared the complete original and revised statements, including hypotheses, quantifiers, conclusions and equality clauses. No unreported loss of a valid assertion found. Unit corrections are documented in the linked unit review.
